idiom_name: sealed interface / sealed class with an exhaustive when
implementation_notes: Kotlin's sealed hierarchies plus an exhaustive when give the pattern's benefit - a new operation without touching the elements - with no accept()/visit() pair: declare the node types as a sealed hierarchy and write each operation as a function whose when covers the hierarchy, and the compiler refuses to compile once a subtype is added. In multiplatform common code an else branch may be required again, since actual platform implementations can add subtypes, which quietly turns the exhaustiveness guarantee back into a runtime concern. The classic visitor interface still applies when the hierarchy must stay open (a sealed hierarchy is closed by definition), when elements must drive the traversal themselves, or when operations are classes with configuration that is passed around.
code_sketch:
sealed interface Shape
data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape
data class Rect(val w: Double, val h: Double) : Shape

fun area(s: Shape): Double = when (s) {      // no else: compiler-checked
    is Circle -> Math.PI * s.r * s.r
    is Rect   -> s.w * s.h
}
// fun perimeter(s: Shape) = when (s) { ... }  // new operation, new function
pitfalls: A when used as a statement with an else silently accepts new subtypes; use the expression form (or omit else) so the compiler enforces coverage.
sealed is not transitive: matching on a subtype that is not itself sealed loses the exhaustiveness check.
A when over a nullable or Any-typed reference needs an else anyway, so erasing the static type at the boundary gives up the guarantee.
In multiplatform projects the common-code when may need an else, because platform actual types are not visible to the compiler there.

variants.name: Classic Visitor interface with accept() and overloaded visit()
variants.idiom_name: interface ShapeVisitor<R> plus accept(visitor) on each element
variants.implementation_notes: The GoF structure translates directly: a Visitor interface with one overloaded visit(shape: Circle) / visit(shape: Rect) per element, and elements implementing accept(visitor) = visitor.visit(this); Kotlin resolves the correct overload because the static type of this inside each element is the concrete class. Choose it over the sealed-when form when the hierarchy cannot be sealed (third-party or intentionally open), when accept() must itself drive the traversal, or when an operation is a configurable object with lifecycle. The price is the classic one, enforced earlier than in Java: a new element type is a missing method, and the compiler demands implementations in every visitor immediately.
pitfalls: Defining accept() on a base class makes this statically the base type, so overload resolution picks the wrong visit() - each element must override it.
Two operations with different result types cannot share one visitor interface unless it is generic in the result type; forgetting R leads to Any and unchecked casts at the call site.
Providing default no-op implementations on the visitor interface is convenient but hides missing cases; require every method when completeness matters.
Visitors holding state must not be shared: a Kotlin object (singleton) as a stateful visitor is a data race across threads or coroutines.
